evidence.label: Counterexamples to the Hahn-Wilson conjecture at height two

headline: A paper claims to disprove the Hahn–Wilson conjecture at height two, for every large enough prime.
scope: Connective p-complete spectra of exact fp-type two, and finite constructions from BP⟨2⟩, for sufficiently large primes p.
plain: The Hahn–Wilson conjecture says a simple algebraic test picks out exactly which infinite spectra can be built from BP⟨n⟩ in finitely many steps. The paper claims a counterexample at height two for every large enough prime. Its spectrum passes the algebraic test but cannot be built from BP⟨2⟩ that way. It also passes two localization tests that were proposed as a possible extra condition. The paper says the problem lies in how the local pieces are glued.
doesNot: This does not cover small primes, and it does not address the conjecture at height three or above.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Jeremy Hahn and Dylan Wilson, conjecture later written down by Lee and Pstrągowski
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to refute a recent conjecture describing which infinite spectra have finite constructions from truncated Brown–Peterson spectra.

explanation:
Fix the prime p = 11. A standard spectrum called BP⟨2⟩ has homotopy built from two variables, v₁ and v₂. Their degrees are 2(p − 1) and 2(p² − 1). For p = 11 that gives degrees 20 and 240. So the coefficients form a polynomial ring in two variables, sitting in degrees 20 and 240. This spectrum is the basic building block in this story.

Some background first. A spectrum is the stable version of a space, the object studied in stable homotopy theory. A thick subcategory is everything you can build from a starting object. You may take finite sums, shifts, cones of maps and retracts, a finite number of times. The question is which infinite spectra you can build from BP⟨n⟩ this way.

The Hahn–Wilson conjecture gives a cohomological answer. It says finite presentation over the Steenrod algebra, plus a height bound, should pick out exactly these spectra[1]. The Steenrod algebra is a standard ring of operations on mod-p cohomology. Finitely presented means described by finitely many generators and relations. Such a spectrum is called fp. Mahowald and Rezk proved an equivalent test. Smashing with some finite spectrum must give only finitely many nonzero homotopy groups, each finite[2]. The height is a level in chromatic homotopy theory. Lee and Pstrągowski wrote the conjecture down and report learning it from Dylan Wilson in 2021[3].

Some cases were known. Lee and Pstrągowski proved the conjecture at height one[4]. A related claim, the telescope conjecture, compares two ways to localize a spectrum. Burklund, Hahn, Levy and Schlank disproved it at every prime and every height of at least two[5]. But those examples fail the fp finiteness test. So they do not give an fp counterexample[6].

The paper claims to disprove the Hahn–Wilson conjecture at height two[7]. For each large enough prime, it builds a spectrum X of exact fp-type two. Yet X cannot be built from BP⟨2⟩ in finitely many steps. The result holds for sufficiently large primes[8]. The spectrum X also passes both localization comparisons. Lee and Pstrągowski had suggested such a hypothesis might be enough. The paper says this extra hypothesis does not suffice at height two[9].

Why is X hard to catch? Its local pieces, seen one height at a time, keep strong finiteness properties. The obstruction lies in how those local pieces are joined[10]. So any local test will pass. Only the global gluing shows that X is not finitely built.

The construction uses chromatic algebraicity. At large primes, spectra can be modelled by sheaves on a stack of formal group laws. The paper uses Pstrągowski's comparison, available at height two for p > 8[11]. Its own operator needs larger primes still[12]. It builds the example by gluing a complete part to an open part, through a carefully chosen map on the overlap.

How sure is this? No Lean check covers this paper. No specialist review has been published. The proof relies on deep comparison theorems, so the counterexample remains a claim.
hypeCheck: Solid if correct. No Lean check and no specialist review; the counterexample depends on deep comparison theorems and holds only for large primes.

glossary.meaning: The stable version of a space; the basic object of stable homotopy theory.
A truncated Brown–Peterson spectrum; its coefficients are polynomials in v₁ to vₙ over the p-adic integers.
Everything you can build from given objects using finite sums, shifts, cones and retracts, finitely many times.
A standard ring of operations that acts on mod-p cohomology of every space or spectrum.
A spectrum whose mod-p cohomology is finitely presented over the Steenrod algebra.
A height attached to an fp spectrum, measured by which finite spectra make its homotopy finite.
A level in chromatic homotopy theory; higher heights see finer information.
A prediction that two ways of localizing at a height agree; it is now known to fail at heights two and above.
